questions.q: Which of these is an SI base unit?
questions.solution: The SI base units you need at A-level are the kilogram, metre, second, ampere, kelvin and mole (the seventh, the candela, is not required). The newton, joule and volt are derived units: each can be written as a combination of base units.

questions.q: What is a capacitance of \(4.7\ \mu\text{F}\) in farads?
questions.solution: The prefix micro means one millionth, \(10^{-6}\). So \(4.7\ \mu\text{F} = 4.7 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{F}\). Milli is \(10^{-3}\) and nano is \(10^{-9}\).

questions.q: What is the joule written in SI base units?
questions.solution: Work is force times distance. Force is mass times acceleration, with units \(\text{kg m s}^{-2}\). Multiplying by a distance in metres gives \(\text{kg m}^{2}\ \text{s}^{-2}\).

questions.q: A micrometer shows a small reading when its jaws are fully closed. If this is not corrected, what kind of error does it cause?
questions.solution: A zero error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, which makes it a systematic error. It is not reduced by repeating readings; it has to be found and subtracted.

questions.q: Which is the best way to reduce the effect of random errors on a measurement?

options.A: Check the instrument for a zero error.
options.B: Use an instrument with a larger range.
options.C: Calibrate the instrument against a standard.
options.D: Repeat the measurement and take a mean.

questions.solution: Random errors scatter readings above and below the true value, so they tend to cancel in a mean of repeated readings. Checking for a zero error and calibrating deal with systematic errors instead.

questions.q: A student measures a quantity several times. The readings are very close to each other but all well below the true value. How should the readings be described?
questions.solution: Precise readings are close to each other, with little spread. Accurate readings are close to the true value. These are close together but far from the true value, which points to a systematic error.

questions.q: A length is measured as 25.0 cm with an uncertainty of 0.5 cm. What is the percentage uncertainty?
questions.solution: Percentage uncertainty is the absolute uncertainty divided by the value, times 100: 0.5 ÷ 25.0 × 100 = 2%.

questions.q: A density is calculated from a mass with a percentage uncertainty of 2% and a volume with a percentage uncertainty of 3%. What is the percentage uncertainty in the density?
questions.solution: When quantities are multiplied or divided, their percentage uncertainties add: 2 + 3 = 5%. Subtracting them (1%) is the usual slip: uncertainties never cancel.

questions.q: The radius of a circle is measured with a percentage uncertainty of 3%. What is the percentage uncertainty in its calculated area?
questions.solution: Area depends on the radius squared. When a quantity is raised to a power, its percentage uncertainty is multiplied by that power: 2 × 3 = 6%.

questions.q: Two lengths are measured as (5.0 ± 0.1) cm and (3.0 ± 0.2) cm. What is the uncertainty in the difference between them?
questions.solution: When quantities are added or subtracted, their absolute uncertainties add, even for a difference: 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 cm. Subtracting the uncertainties (0.1 cm) is the usual slip.

questions.q: Which is the best estimate of the mass of an apple?
questions.solution: An apple has a mass of roughly 100 g. In kilograms: 100 ÷ 1000 = 0.1 kg. An estimate only needs to be right to the nearest order of magnitude.

questions.q: What is meant by the resolution of a measuring instrument?

options.A: The smallest change in the quantity that the instrument can show.
options.B: The largest value the instrument can measure.
options.C: How close its readings are to the true value.
options.D: How close repeated readings are to each other.

questions.solution: Resolution is the smallest change in the quantity being measured that gives a change in the reading, for example 1 mm on a ruler marked in millimetres. Closeness to the true value is accuracy; closeness of repeats is precision.
